name: 15th Five-Year Plan for Addressing Climate Change
status: Published on 27 July 2026, implementation in progress.
background: Statutory directives under China's 15th Five-Year Plan framework and national climate strategies in order to guarantee the 2030 carbon peaking target, accomplish Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), and strengthen China's leadership in global climate governance.
key_implication: It imposes operational restrictions on businesses, including mandatory coal consumption replacement limits, phased-out inefficient capacities, and strict carbon footprint reporting, while providing financial incentives through expanded carbon market trading, green finance access, and green certificate monetization.
framings: Agriculture; Oil and gas; Coal; Accelerating Green-Low Carbon Transition; Carbon Market; N2O Emission Control; Fluorinated Gas Controls; Methane Emission Control; Emissions Trading System; Clean Energy; Municipal Waste/Wastewater Control; Digital Infrastructure; Carbon Market Digitisation; Carbon Footprint Management System; Ecological Carbon Sinks; Science, AI & carbon capture, usage and storage

name: 15th Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the People's Republic of China
status: Guides China's development priorities in the 2026-2030 period.
background: Responds to the profound and complex changes in the international landscape alongside interwoven structural and cyclical domestic imbalances during the conclusion of the 14th Five-Year Plan in order to lay a solid foundation for achieving Chinese-style modernization and the nation's 2035 economic, technological, and strategic developmental goals.
key_implication: This national blueprint creates incentives by opening strategic market scenarios in emerging sectors, driving state capital and patient financing into 'hard tech' innovations, and establishing enhanced tax deductions for corporate R&D. Conversely, it enforces restrictions by subjecting high-risk AI models and algorithms to mandatory security assessments, implementing strict energy and carbon-accounting boundaries across traditional supply chains, and banning non-compliant market-splitting actions via anti-monopoly local protectionism rules.

advanced semiconductor wafer fabrication equipment, precision lithography/deposition components, brain-computer interface medical components, high-end medical devices such as CT scanners, high-resolution MRI and surgical robots; Large cruise ships, large LNG carriers, CR450 high-speed standard bullet trains; reusable heavy-lift launch vehicles, commercial satellites, C919/C929 commercial airliner production, large payload fixed-wing drones, and eVTOL aircraft; High-performance motors/control systems, gas turbines, high-head large-capacity hydroelectric generator units; advanced new power batteries such as high-capacity electrodes, electrolytes, composite current collectors for EVs and smart terminals; Advanced general-purpose foundational optoelectronic and sensing components; Mature and advanced node integrated circuits, high-performance AI processors/chips, high-density storage, brain-computer interface electrodes, and quantum processing units; Online efficient intelligent testing systems, extreme environment adjustments, high-performance flow measurements, quantum and in-situ calibration meters; Large-scale hydro, wind, and solar integrated bases, "Gobi/Desert/Wilderness" multi-energy networks, deep-sea wind arrays, 4th-generation nuclear reactors, and high-voltage cross-regional clean energy transmission grids; Green hydrogen infrastructure, pipeline network layout, and natural gas integration; "Eight Vertical and Eight Horizontal" high-speed passenger rail trunk lines, Sichuan-Tibet railway system, multi-modal container freight nodes; National highway networks, strategic border highways (G219, G331), and coastal transport routes (G228); World-class sea-port cluster systems (Yangshan, Ningbo-Zhoushan, Nansha), Three Gorges deep-water route upgrades, and high-tier inland river shipping networks; name: 15th Five-Year Plan for Modernising the National Emergency Management System (State Council No. 15 of 2026)
status: Published on 20 May 2026, implementation in progress.
background: Responds to the strategic requirement of aligning public safety and disaster mitigation with China's 15th Five-Year Plan in order to establish a proactive, modernised, and intelligence-driven national emergency management system focused on risk prevention and disaster resilience by 2035.
key_implication: It imposes regulatory compliance restrictions by mandating all-chain safety inspections, dynamic "ban/restrict/control" negative lists, and strict administrative enforcement ("double-penalty" fines and criminal prosecution) across high-risk sectors such as chemicals, mining, and ultra-high-rise construction. Conversely, it establishes economic incentives for compliant businesses, offering government financing guarantees, preferential funding, fast-track adoption for "first-set" major technical equipment, and rewards for internal hazard reporting.
framings: Specialised Emergency Compliance, Industrial Enforcement and Municipal Fire Safety Services; Industrial Chemical Risk Identification, Park Safety Management and Retrofit Engineering; Deep-Coal Mining Extraction Safety, Hazard Mitigation and Structural Retrofitting Services; Specialised Emergency Machinery, Fire-Rescue Robotics anmd Disaster Detection Equipment Manufacturing; Industrial AI Architecture, Emergency LLM Deployment & Remote Sensing Data Services

name: 15th Five-Year Plan for Renewable Energy Development (National Development and Reform Commission and National Energy Administration No. 1067 of 2026)
status: Published on 6 July 2026, implementation in progress
background: Responds to the strategic mandate of accelerating comprehensive green economic transition and achieving reliable fossil-fuel substitution during the 15th Five-Year Plan period in order to scale up renewable energy supply, enhance grid integration quality, and fulfill China's 2030 carbon peaking commitments.
key_implication: It imposes regulatory restrictions by establishing mandatory minimum renewable energy consumption quotas across major energy-consuming industries and enforcing strict grid-connection technical standards (including a minimum 10% firm capacity requirement for new wind and solar farms). Conversely, it creates substantial economic incentives by fast-tracking administrative permitting for integrated multi-energy and microgrid projects, expanding green-certificate trading revenue streams, and implementing capacity payment mechanisms for energy storage and grid-flexibility providers.
framings: Multi-Energy Integrated Energy Hubs, Deep-Offshore Wind Development and Grid Decarbonization Systems; Advanced Solar PV, Ultra-Large Wind Turbines, Grid-Forming Inverters and Long-Duration Storage Hardware Manufacturing; Renewable Hydrogen Production, Green Ammonia and Green Methanol Chemical Synthesis Clusters; Smart Energy Forecasting Algorithms, Virtual Power Plants (VPP), Smart Microgrids and Digital-Twin Power Infrastructure; Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Synthesis, Non-Grain Biofuel Refining and Industrial Green Fuel Substitution

status: Effective from 22 June 2026.
background: Aims to stabilise foreign investment and resolve market access or operational barriers across key service, financial, and industrial sectors in order to expand China's high-level opening up and fully optimise the quality of foreign capital utilisation.

name: Announcement on the EU Foreign Subsidies Investigation Constituting Improper Extraterritorial Jurisdiction (Ministry of Justice Notice No. 5 of 2026)
status: Effective from 15 May 2026.
background: Responds to the European Union utilising its Foreign Subsidies Regulation to conduct cross-border data and asset investigations into Nuctech (同方威视) in order to legally block foreign unilateral data gathering and safeguard the commercial information security of Chinese corporate entities from discriminatory economic protectionism.
key_implication: This is the first case covered by the Regulations on Countermeasures against Foreign States' Unlawful Extraterritorial Jurisdiction. This announcement imposes an absolute restriction by completely banning any domestic organisation or individual from executing or assisting with the European Union's cross-border investigation under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR). It offers zero commercial or regulatory incentives, placing multinational companies under immediate legal jeopardy if they attempt to comply with EU information disclosure requests while operating within China.
framings: Manufacture of high-tech screening infrastructure; Banks; Corporate legal defense practices, auditing firms, and compliance consultancies

name: Announcement on the EU Foreign Subsidies Investigation Constituting Improper Extraterritorial Jurisdiction (Ministry of Justice Notice No.8  of 2026)
status: In force since 19 August 2026.
background: Responds to the cross-border investigative actions taken by the European Union against JD.com under its Foreign Subsidies Regulation in order to block the enforcement of improper extraterritorial jurisdictions and safeguard the legal rights of Chinese business entities.
key_implication: This is the second case covered by the "Regulations on Countermeasures against Foreign States' Unlawful Extraterritorial Jurisdiction" within 3 months. It established a strict legal ban prohibiting all organizations and individuals from executing or assisting with the EU’s cross-border investigative measures under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation. This creates an immediate compliance conflict for businesses operating across both jurisdictions, legally blocking them from complying with European regulatory demands while within China.
framings: Large-scale e-commerce platforms and digital service conglomerates; Digital logistics infrastructure, cloud services, and enterprise software systems handling cross-border corporate information; Banks; Third-party compliance firms, law firms, and consulting agencies

name: China Adds 14 EU Entities to Export Control List (Ministry of Commerce No.30 of 2026)
status: In force since 24 July 2026.
background: The European Council adopted its 21st package of sanctions for the Ukraine-Russia war, in which 14 Chinese entities were involved, on July 23, 2026. China responded the next day, which included 14 European entities mainly in the defence industry. It responded to proliferation risks and geopolitical friction involving targeted European defence, aerospace, and high-tech industrial entities in order to safeguard China's national security interests and rigorously enforce the Export Control Law regarding dual-use items.
key_implication: It prohibits domestic export operators from selling dual-use items to 14 blacklisted EU entities, while introducing an administrative restriction requiring case-by-case Ministry of Commerce approval under exceptional circumstances. name: Cloud and AI Development Act
status: Currently in its European Parliament preparatory stage with the Committee on Industry, Research and Energy and the Committee on the Internal Market and Consumer Protection.
background: The proposal is part of the Tech Sovereignty Package, as well as the AI Continent Action Plan,  and it responds to the 2024 Draghi report and subsequent European Parliament and Council assessments. The Cloud and AI Development Act establishes a unified legal framework to build Union-level computing capacity, bolster industrial competitiveness, and mitigate strategic reliance on non-EU digital infrastructure amid mounting geopolitical fragmentation.
key_implication: The regulation accelerates local digital infrastructure growth by streamlining environmental and resource permitting for data centres while prioritising native European cloud deployment in essential sectors to curb reliance on foreign providers. It establishes a four-tier cloud sovereignty assurance scheme that restricts public sector and critical infrastructure procurement to certified providers, effectively channeling high-security contracts toward European Union suppliers or audited joint ventures.

name: Commission Recommendation on Outbound Investment Screening
status: Member States are submitting their final national transaction reports and risk assessments to the Commission, laying the data groundwork for an EU-wide policy proposal expected by late 2026.
background: Building on the 2024 White Paper and public consultations under the European Economic Security Strategy, Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/63 formally initiates a 15-month fact-finding and data-gathering exercise, directing Member States to monitor and assess risks of technology leakage to third countries from outbound corporate investments in advanced semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and quantum technologies.
key_implication: The framework establishes a retroactive data-gathering and risk-assessment obligation for corporate entities, requiring the tracking of outbound transactions—including venture capital, joint ventures, and intellectual property transfers—dating back to January 2021 within the semiconductor, artificial intelligence, and quantum technology sectors.

name: Council Recommendation on Enhancing Research Security
status: Passed in May 2024, the framework is midway through its 2025–2027 ERA Policy Agenda timeline; following the rollouts of mandatory research security self-assessment pilots by national funding bodies in early 2026, the Commission is launching a centralized European Centre of Expertise and a digital due diligence screening platform by late 2026.
background: As a core element of the European Economic Security Strategy, the Recommendation establishes a coordinated EU framework to protect international academic cooperation against foreign interference and unwanted knowledge transfer by integrating security-vetting and risk-management protocols into national research funding mechanisms.
key_implication: The framework systematically targets asymmetric technology transfers and 'civil-military fusion' risks involving the EU's competitors, effectively subjecting joint academic partnerships, dual-use deep-tech laboratories, and foreign research personnel to heightened, mandatory national security vetting and grant-eligibility restrictions.
framings: Research performing organisations; Research funding organisations

name: Critical Entities Resilience Directive
status: Entering into force on 16 January 2023, the CER Directive set a mandatory Member State national transposition deadline of 17 October 2024 (repealing Directive 2008/114/EC on 18 October 2024), leading into the formal national designation of critical entities by 17 July 2026, with initial Commission compliance and review reports scheduled for July 2027 and June 2029 respectively.
background: Updating the 2008 European Critical Infrastructure framework, the Critical Entities Resilience Directive shifts the EU legal regime from protecting isolated physical assets to reinforcing systemic, cross-sectoral operational resilience for entities delivering essential societal and economic services against complex hybrid, cyber, climate, and terrorism threats.
key_implication: By establishing a standardised non-exhaustive list of essential services across eleven critical sectors, the European Commission provides the mandatory baseline for Member States to conduct risk assessments and officially designate their national critical entities by 17 July 2026, triggering enforceable operational resilience and risk-mitigation obligations for designated operators.

name: Critical Raw Materials Act
status: The initial 2024 regulation is fully active, while a package of targeted 2025 amendments—expanding permanent magnet recycling parameters and shift-assigning corporate supply-chain audit oversight to the Commission—is currently under active interinstitutional negotiation following the Council’s March 2026 position and the Parliament's April 2026 review.
background: Responds to the 2022 Versailles Declaration and growing supply security risks by embedding raw material resilience into the Green Deal Industrial Plan to accelerate internal net-zero technology manufacturing and end strategic dependencies on concentrated foreign imports.

background: Replacing a decade-old strategic baseline to adapt to economic and political developments involving China, this Joint Communication established an updated policy framework for EU engagement centered on reciprocal market access, level-playing-field economic competition, principled defense of human rights and international law, and reinforced internal EU unity across Member State bilateral relations.
key_implication: The Joint Communication shifted the EU’s baseline to an interest-driven policy focusing on economic reciprocity, level-playing-field conditions, and Member State cohesion. It preceded the EU's defensive trade and economic security architecture.

name: EU Steel Regulation

name: The Plan on implementing the Employment-first Strategy (The State Council 2026 No.16)
status: Published on 11 June 2026, implementation in progress
background: Responds to structural labor supply-demand mismatches, rapid technological disruptions from artificial intelligence, and potential unemployment risks during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) in order to promote high-quality full employment, optimise modern human resource allocation, and construct an employment-friendly macroeconomic development framework.
key_implication: It provides economic incentives by expanding direct training subsidies, fiscal support, and targeted funding for enterprises that expand hiring or innovate within emerging and AI-driven sectors. Conversely, it imposes regulatory restrictions by mandating algorithmic transparency and strict labor compliance for platform operators, tightening wage enforcement, and subjecting major investment projects to employment-impact assessments.
framings: AI Bases, Vocational Placement and Market Integrity; "AI+" Deployment and Algorithmic Transparency; Vocational training, enterprise-led apprenticeship models, and university curricula alignment of with strategic emerging industries; Gig-Economy Platforms; Care Networks and Domestic Services

name: White Paper on Export Controls
status: Adopted. The core objectives of the White Paper have been structurally operationalized via the European Commission's adoption of autonomous Delegated Regulations that complement deadlocked multilateral regimes to unilaterally expand the EU's dual-use control list for advanced technologies.
background: Released as part of the 2024 Economic Security Package, this initiative proposes to modernise the EU's dual-use export control framework by introducing fast-track mechanisms for unilateral EU-wide control lists and establishing cross-notification requirements to better coordinate national security restrictions across Member States.
key_implication: The framework shifts dual-use technology oversight toward an autonomous EU-level mechanism, enabling rapid harmonisation of export restrictions on emerging technologies independent of deadlocked multilateral regimes.
framings: Nuclear materials, facilities and equipment; Special materials and related equipment; Materials processing; Electronics; Computers; Telecommunications and 'information security'; Sensors and lasers; Navigation and avionics; Marine; Aerospace and propulsion
